name: Luoyang
info: Luoyang is a city in western Henan province, China, at the confluence of the Luo and Yellow rivers, founded as Chengzhou in 1036 BCE and later the capital of the Eastern Han, Wei, Jin and Northern Wei dynasties.

facts.founded: A settlement named Chengzhou was constructed in 1036 BCE by the Duke of Zhou for the remnants of the captured Shang nobility.
facts.where: At the confluence of the Luo River and the Yellow River in the west of Henan province, on the central plain of China.
facts.known: Chengzhou and Wangcheng of the Zhou; the capital of the Eastern Han, Wei, Jin and Northern Wei; the Longmen Grottoes; the Yongning Temple pagoda; Dongdu of the Tang; Shendu under Wu Zetian; the burnings and sackings of 189, 190, 311 and 534
facts.today: Luoyang is a prefecture-level city in Henan province, China, with about seven million people in its municipality.

t: A settlement called Chengzhou was built in 1036 BCE for captured Shang nobles, and the Eastern Zhou later made Wangcheng, 15 km to its west, and then Chengzhou itself their capital.
Luoyang was the capital of the Eastern Han from 25 CE and was burned, ransacked or sacked in 189, 190, 311 and 534, each time recovering or being rebuilt, as under the Wei in 220 and the Sui in 604.

Under the Northern Wei, Sui, Tang and Song it was successively a capital, the Eastern Capital and the Western Capital, with populations of 600,000 under the Jin and the Northern Wei and around one million under the Tang.
dyk: In 166 CE the first Roman mission, sent by the king of Da Qin, Andun, reached Luoyang after arriving by sea in what later became central Vietnam. Andun is identified as Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, who reigned from 161 to 180.
ev: The Duke of Zhou builds Chengzhou for the remnants of the captured Shang nobility
Wangcheng becomes the capital of the Eastern Zhou
Emperor Guangwu declares Luoyang the capital of the Eastern Han
The Han capital is burned in the civil war that followed the Yellow Turban rebellion
Han-Zhao forces sack and raze the city in the Disaster of Yongjia
Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei moves his capital from Datong to Luoyang
Gao Huan destroys the city and moves its population to Ye
Emperor Yang of Sui founds a new Luoyang on the site of the existing city

sections.origins:
Luoyang lies in the west of Henan province, in the confluence area of the Luo River and the Yellow River, on the central plain of China. Its name comes from its position on the north, or sunny ("yang"), side of the Luo River: the river flows from west to east and the sun stands to its south, so the sun always shines on the north bank. Among its earlier names were Luoyi and Luozhou.

In 1036 BCE a settlement named Chengzhou was constructed by the Duke of Zhou for the remnants of the captured Shang nobility. The Duke also moved the Nine Tripod Cauldrons to Chengzhou from the Zhou capital at Haojing. A second Western Zhou capital, Wangcheng, also called Luoyi, was built 15 km west of Chengzhou. The Eastern Han capital of Luoyang was later built over Chengzhou, while the modern city is built over the ruins of Wangcheng, which are visible at Wangcheng Park.
sections.growth:
Wangcheng became the capital of the Eastern Zhou dynasty in 771 BCE, and in 510 BCE the Eastern Zhou capital was moved to Chengzhou. Qin Shi Huang's chief minister, Lu Buwei, was given Luoyang and began programmes to develop and beautify it.

The city rose again after the Han. The Jin dynasty was established in Luoyang, and at the height of Jin rule it had a population of 600,000 and was probably the second largest city in the world after Rome. Under the Northern Wei it reached a population of 600,000 at its height. Emperor Xiaowen moved more than 150,000 people to the site by 495 and began the rock-cut Longmen Grottoes, in which more than 30,000 Buddhist statues from the dynasty's time have been found. The Yongning Temple, the tallest pagoda in China, was also built there, and the Shaolin Temple was built by the emperor to accommodate an Indian monk on Mount Song next to the city.

Under the Tang, as Dongdu, the Eastern Capital, Luoyang had a population of around one million at its height, second only to Chang'an, then the largest city in the world.
sections.rulers:
It is said that Liu Bang visited Luoyang and considered making it his capital but was persuaded by his ministers to choose Chang'an. On 27 November 25 CE Emperor Guangwu of Han declared Luoyang the capital of the Eastern Han dynasty. After the court moved west to Chang'an and the warlord Cao Cao held the last Han emperor, Xian, at Xuchang from 196 to 220, Cao Pi, Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty, declared Luoyang his capital in 220. The Jin dynasty, successor to Wei, was also established there.

For the next two centuries Luoyang was a contested region. In 328 it was the site of a battle between the Han-Zhao and Later Zhao dynasties that established the latter as a hegemonic power in the north. In the winter of 416 the Jin general Tan Daoji took it during Liu Yu's northern expedition against the Later Qin. The Xianbei-led Northern Wei captured it in 422, the Liu Song recovered it in 430, and by the 460s it was definitively under Wei control.

Emperor Yang of Sui took control in 604. Under the Tang the city was Dongdu, and for a time Empress Wu moved the capital of her Zhou dynasty there and named it Shendu, the divine capital. Under the Northern Song it was the Western Capital, Xijing, and the birthplace of Zhao Kuangyin, the founder of the Song dynasty. It was later renamed Henanfu and regained its former name in 1912.
sections.life:
The Eastern Han walls formed a rectangle 4 km from south to north and 2.5 km from west to east, with the Gu River, a tributary of the Luo, just outside the northern and eastern walls. The rectangular Southern Palace and Northern Palace stood 3 km apart and were connected by the Covered Way. In 26 CE the Altar of the Gods of the Soils and Grains, the Altar of Heaven and the Temple of the Founder, Emperor Gao of Former Han, were inaugurated, the Imperial University was restored in 29, the Yang Canal linked the capital to the Luo in 48, and the main imperial observatory, the Spiritual Terrace, was built in 56. When Emperor Yang of Sui founded the new Luoyang in 604 he used a layout inspired by his father Emperor Wen's work in rebuilding Chang'an.

Under the Tang the city had Christians among its people. Epitaphs record Lady An, a Nestorian Christian Sogdian woman who died in 821, and her Han Chinese husband Hua Xian, who died in 827, and another Sogdian woman, also surnamed An, buried by her military officer son on 22 January 815. The sons of such marriages became civil officials and military officers, and neither their mixed ancestry nor their faith was a barrier to their careers. During the Northern Song the city served as a cultural centre that housed some philosophers.
sections.crises:
The Yellow Turban rebellion, defeated by imperial troops in 184, weakened the Han state until rebellions turned into civil war. The Han capital of Luoyang was burned on 24 September 189. On 4 April 190 Chancellor Dong Zhuo ordered his soldiers to ransack, pillage and raze the city as he retreated from a coalition of regional lords, and the court was moved to the more defensible Chang'an. Luoyang was restored to prominence when Cao Pi made it his capital in 220.

At the start of the 4th century the city suffered repeated attacks during the War of the Eight Princes and the Upheaval of the Five Barbarians under the Jin. In 311 rebel forces of the Xiongnu-led Han-Zhao dynasty sacked and razed it in the event known as the Disaster of Yongjia.

The Northern Wei city was destroyed in 534 by the warlord Gao Huan, who captured it and forced its population to move to his capital at Ye. Under the Tang, Luoyang was damaged during the An Lushan Rebellion.
sections.legacy:
Luoyang is among the oldest cities in China and one of the cradles of Chinese civilisation, and it is the earliest of the Four Great Ancient Capitals of China. The Longmen Grottoes were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2000. In 2014 UNESCO also listed three sites at Luoyang under the Silk Roads, the Han Wei Luoyang City Site, the Dingding Gate Site of Sui Tang Luoyang City and the Xin'an Hangu Guan Site, and two sites of the Grand Canal, the Huiluo Barn and the Hanjia Barn. The Luoyang Museum, established in 1958, displays relics from the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties.

Luoyang today is governed as a prefecture-level city bordering the provincial capital of Zhengzhou to the east. The built-up area was held in the 2010 census to have 1,857,003 people, and the whole municipality 6,549,941. In 2021 Yanshi City became an urban district and Jili District and Mengjin County were merged into Mengjin District, which effectively doubled the urban area. The city's peonies and a 24-course dish, the Luoyang Water Banquet, are among the traditions associated with it.

summary: Luoyang, on the Luo and Yellow rivers in Henan, began as Chengzhou in 1036 BCE and was a capital of the Eastern Zhou, Eastern Han, Wei, Jin and Northern Wei, and the Eastern Capital of the Tang. It was repeatedly burned and rebuilt, and is now a city of about seven million people.
references: Arthur Cotterell, The Imperial Capitals of China: An Inside View of the Celestial Empire (Pimlico, 2008)
W. J. Jenner, Memories of Loyang (Clarendon Press, 1981)
notes: Only the city's own article was available; no Luoyang history article.
Start: the article gives 1036 BC for Chengzhou; kept as -1036 without circa.
Wei capital: the article says the Han court moved to Chang'an after 190 and that Cao Cao held Emperor Xian at Xuchang (196-220); I did not call Chang'an or Xuchang capitals beyond that.
Burning of 189 (24 September) and ransacking of 190 (4 April) are both stated; I told both and used 189 for the event.

Population: Jin 600,000 and Northern Wei 600,000 are given as such, the Jin figure with 'probably the second largest city in the world after Rome'; Tang about one million. The Tang figure is 'around one million'.

The Wu Zetian section: the article says the Zhou capital was moved to Luoyang and named Shen Du; the tallest palace in Chinese history claim was left out. The name Shendu also appears in the Etymology section.

Left out as promotional or doubtful: the culture section's claims that Luoyang is the foundation of Confucianism, birth of Taoism, origin of the compass, paper and printing, Hakka ancestry and 70% of clan names; the Gaocheng observatory (80 km away); cuisine, subway, climate, tourist numbers and the conservation lab.
The 166 CE Roman mission is as the article gives it; the article's wording 'arriving by sea in Rinan Commandery in what later is central Vietnam' is paraphrased.

The Etymology section's name list says Luoyang was 'later renamed Henanfu until regained its former name in 1912' without dates for the rename; I gave only 1912. It also calls the Song name Xijing; the History section calls it the Western Capital.
Tang Christian epitaph paragraph: I left out the article's stereotypes about Hu women and its speculation on why Han men married Sogdian women.
The Han-era Yang Canal is given as linking the capital to the Luo in 48 CE.
